title: Rebekah says "I will go" (Genesis 24:57–58)
hookLine: her family asks her, and she chooses for herself

cards: Rebekah runs home and tells her family about the stranger at the well. Her brother Laban sees the gold bracelets, and invites the servant in.
Food is set out, and the servant says: I won't eat until I've told you why I'm here. And he tells the whole story again, every detail: the prayer, the camels, the water.
The rabbis noticed how long the Torah lets him talk, and said even the everyday speech of the patriarchs' servants is precious. The family agrees to the match.
But in the morning, when the servant wants to leave, her mother and brother hesitate: let her stay with us a while, ten days at least. Don't hold me back, the servant says.

teach.b: In the old JPS translation, they say: "We will call the damsel, and inquire at her mouth." They ask her directly: "Wilt thou go with this man?"
She answers in one Hebrew word, elech: "I will go." Two things to notice. First, the asking.

Rashi, the medieval commentator, reads this verse as a law: from here we learn that a woman may not be married off without her consent. Jewish law, as it developed, holds that a grown woman's marriage needs her own yes.
The Torah could have skipped her answer. Instead it pauses to show someone asking her first. Second, the answer.

Some commentators notice that Rebekah's yes sounds like Abraham's call: she, too, leaves her land, her birthplace and her father's house, for a man and a place she's never seen. She goes before she knows, just as he did.

teach.h: WILT THOU GO WITH THIS MAN?
teach.b: Her family sends her off with a blessing: our sister, may you become thousands upon thousands. At the bedeken, a Jewish wedding custom, those words are said to the bride as her veil is lowered.
At the chapter's end, she arrives. Isaac has gone out to the field at evening, the Torah says, to meditate. She sees him from her camel and veils herself.
He brings her into his mother Sarah's tent, and he loves her, the Torah says plainly, and he is comforted after his mother's death. And it started with a question: will you go?

how: At Jewish weddings that keep the bedeken, the veiling of the bride, the blessing Rebekah's family gave her is said over the bride; Jewish law requires the bride's own consent to the marriage.

games.q: you're Rebekah. a stranger has come from far away, your family has agreed, and now they turn to you: wilt thou go with this man? what do you say?
games.why: one Hebrew word, elech: I will go. like Abraham, she leaves land and father's house for a place she's never seen.

practice: Think of a good invitation you keep not answering: a dinner you've been putting off, a class, a trip, a phone call, a new friendship, a volunteer shift.
Notice what holds you back, tiredness, fear, habit, then picture answering like Rebekah, with one short word: I'll go. If you pray, you can ask for a clear yes.
